1107.title: the Lalita Sahasranama (selections)
1107.hook: who wrote the names? the story inside the text: goddesses of speech, a crowded court, and a hymn handed to everyone
1107.howItsDone: Some devotees learn the Lalita Sahasranama from a teacher and recite it daily or on Fridays; in a temple or home archana, a name is offered with each flower or pinch of kumkum, in the form 'om … namah.'

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lalita Sahasranama held two ways of speaking side by side: won over by devotion, and without form. A new week.
screen: `NEAR, AND WITHOUT.`

segments.voice: The court is full. Gods, goddesses, sages and attendants are packed in before the throne of the goddess Lalita. Then the goddesses of speech step forward and begin to recite, name after name. That's the scene the Brahmanda Purana gives for where the Lalita Sahasranama came from. The whole hymn is set inside a conversation: Hayagriva, a horse-headed form of Vishnu, teaching the sage Agastya. And when Agastya hears the names, he's also told how they began, and what the goddess did when she heard them.
screen: `A FULL COURT.` → `THE GODDESSES OF SPEECH.` → `WHO WROTE THE NAMES?`

segments.voice: Here's the story, in paraphrase, as the text tells it. Lalita calls the goddesses of speech, the Vagdevis, Vashini and her companions, and asks them to compose a hymn of her secret names, so that her devotees might have a way to please her. They compose it. Then one day, with the whole court gathered, the goddess signals to them, and the Vagdevis stand and recite the names they've made. The court is amazed. And the goddess, pleased, tells everyone assembled to recite it: this hymn, made at her command, is the way to her favor. Two things are worth a second look. First, the authors. In the story the names weren't put together by a poet at a desk. They came from the goddesses of speech themselves, and some readers take that as the reason the hymn is honored the way it is: speech itself, praising the one it comes from. Second, what happens to the hymn. It begins as something called secret, composed in a palace, and by the end of the scene it's handed to a whole roomful of beings, with an instruction to use it. The story doesn't treat the names as a treasure to lock away. Tradition does keep some reverence around them; some teachers say the hymn should be received from a teacher, not picked up casually. Both live side by side. But the scene itself ends with the doors open: a hymn of praise, commissioned by the one being praised, and then given away.
screen: `LALITA CALLS THE GODDESSES OF SPEECH.` · `THEY COMPOSE HER SECRET NAMES.` · `THEY RECITE THEM IN THE FULL COURT.` · `SHE TELLS EVERYONE TO RECITE IT.` · then, large: `COMMISSIONED, THEN GIVEN AWAY.`

segments.voice: Choose one name from the hymn that you've met this week, the one who gives grace, the one fond of devotion, the one without form, or simply the name Lalita, and say it once, quietly. Let the silence after it be as long as the name, then say it again, unhurried. If you pray, you can offer the name back to the goddess each time; if you don't, notice what a single word does when it's given room.
The Lalita Sahasranama. In the text's own story, composed by the goddesses of speech at Lalita's command, and given to everyone in her court.
screen: `THE LALITA SAHASRANAMA — today's word`.

1108.title: the Lalita Sahasranama (selections)
1108.hook: the hymn's last names: Shiva and Shakti as one form, and then the mother, Lalitambika
1108.howItsDone: In recitation of the Lalita Sahasranama the closing names, Sri Shiva, Shivashaktyaikyarupini and Lalitambika, end the hymn, and in a name-by-name archana the last offering is made with the name Lalitambika.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lalita Sahasranama's own story: the goddesses of speech composed it, and Lalita gave it to her whole court. Today, the last of the names.
screen: `COMPOSED, THEN GIVEN AWAY.`

segments.voice: Some strings of prayer beads have a larger bead where the two ends meet. Move bead by bead and the fingers come back to it: the end of the round is where it started. The Lalita Sahasranama has a shape a little like that. It opens by calling the goddess Sri Mata, the auspicious mother. And after everything in between, the hands, the war, the five acts, the climb through the body, the names of without, it closes on the mother again.
screen: `A BEAD WHERE THE ENDS MEET.` → `IT OPENS WITH THE MOTHER.` → `IT CLOSES ON HER AGAIN.`

segments.voice: The final names, in paraphrase. Sri Shiva: the auspicious one, given the very name of Shiva. Then: the one whose form is the oneness of Shiva and Shakti. And last: Lalitambika, Lalita the mother. Take the middle one first. Shiva and Shakti can sound like two: the god and the goddess, consciousness and its power, the still one and the one who moves. This name says they have a single form, and that form is hers. The poet Kalidasa, at the opening of one of his poems, pictures the divine couple joined like a word and its meaning. Nobody can hold the meaning in one hand and the word in the other. That's the oneness the name points at. Then the very last name. Tradition hears play in the name Lalita, or loveliness, and amba is mother. So the hymn that began with the auspicious mother ends with the playful mother. Between those bookends sit the noose of desire and the goad of anger, a war, Kama brought back from ash, the hidden and the given, a power rising through the spine, and names that say no form can hold her. After all that, the last word isn't a throne or a weapon or an abstraction. It's mother. Some devotees hear a homecoming in that: however far the names travel, they end at the one who looks after you. Others hear the oneness in the name before it: the mother at the end is the whole of reality, playing. Tomorrow the path carries the goddess into her nine nights.

segments.voice: Notice the turn at the top and the bottom of each breath: each one ends where the next begins, like beads on a string. Near the end, bring to mind someone who has looked after you, and let the breath come round to them. If you pray, you can say the name Lalitambika, or the name you use for the one who holds you, once, quietly; if you don't, let the breath be the bead.
The Lalita Sahasranama. A hymn that opens with the auspicious mother and closes with Lalitambika, Lalita the mother.

1109.title: Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum
1109.hook: night one: seeds in a clay dish, a pot of water, and a festival that works like a course taken in order
1109.howItsDone: In some North Indian homes the first day of Navaratri begins with ghatasthapana: a water pot is installed for the goddess and barley is sown in soil to sprout through the nine nights; elsewhere the first night opens with dance, a display of dolls, or recitation of the Devi Mahatmya.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lalita Sahasranama closed on Lalitambika, Lalita the mother. Tonight, the goddess's nine nights begin.
screen: `THE LAST WORD IS MOTHER.` → `THE NINE NIGHTS BEGIN.`

segments.voice: In some homes in North India, the first night of Navaratri starts with dirt. A shallow clay dish, a layer of soil, a handful of barley seeds pressed in. A pot of water is set beside it, or on it, with mango leaves and a coconut at its mouth, and a lamp is lit. Night by night, almost nothing seems to happen. Then something does: by the end of the festival, the dish is full of thin green shoots. Nine nights, and a lesson you can watch grow.
screen: `SOIL, SEEDS, A POT OF WATER.` → `NIGHT BY NIGHT.` → `A LESSON YOU CAN WATCH GROW.`

segments.voice: You met these nights on day eighty. Now, the nights taken in order. Navaratri means nine nights, and they belong to the goddess. There's more than one Navaratri in the year; the one this path keeps falls in autumn. And the Devi Mahatmya, read whole at the start of this year, points at that season. Near its end the goddess says, in paraphrase: at the great worship held in autumn, whoever hears this story of mine with devotion will be freed from troubles. So for some households the nights are also a reading plan, the Devi Mahatmya recited across them. Why call it a curriculum? The nights aren't nine copies of one evening. They come in order, like a course. In some places each night has its own form of the goddess, its own color, its own offerings. Families don't all keep it the same way, and regions differ a great deal: dancing in one place, a staircase of dolls in another, great images of Durga in another. But underneath, the shape repeats. You begin, you stay, and the staying does the work. One way of counting gives the first nights to Durga, the one who faces down whatever blocks the road. That makes night one the first day of school: you just show up and plant something. Nobody expects shoots tonight. The seed is sown so the coming nights have something to tend. The curriculum begins with a beginning, and trusts the rest to time.
screen: `NINE NIGHTS FOR THE GODDESS.` · `HEAR MY STORY IN AUTUMN.` · `IN ORDER, LIKE A COURSE.` · `NIGHT ONE: SHOW UP AND PLANT.` · then, large: `A BEGINNING, TRUSTED TO TIME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small thing you'd like to grow over the next nine nights, not a resolution but a seed: a little more patience at dinner, ten minutes of reading, calling your grandmother. Hold it lightly, like a seed between two fingers, then set it down in good soil and leave it there. If you pray, you can offer it to the goddess on this first night, in your own words; if you don't, simply let it be planted.
Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum. Nine nights for the goddess, kept in order like a course. Night one: show up, and plant something.

1110.title: Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum
1110.hook: night two: Durga's nights, and a hymn that calls her both a hard place and the boat across
1110.howItsDone: During the first nights of Navaratri, some families keep a fast, light a lamp before an image of Durga, visit her temple, or recite chapters of the Devi Mahatmya, including the gods' hymn of praise in chapter four.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-TEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday was night one of Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum: show up, and plant something. Tonight, night two.
screen: `NIGHT ONE: SHOW UP AND PLANT.`

segments.voice: What does a hard stretch of life need: a wall, or a boat? A wall keeps trouble out. A boat gets you through it. Night two sits inside the first stretch of nights, the ones that, in one way of counting, belong to Durga, the goddess who faces down whatever blocks the road. And a verse in the Devi Mahatmya, sung by the gods after her great victory, plays on her name. Some readers hear a wall and a boat in it at once.
screen: `A WALL, OR A BOAT?` → `THE CLEARING NIGHTS.` → `A NAME WITH TWO MEANINGS.`

segments.voice: In the fourth chapter of the Devi Mahatmya, the buffalo demon has fallen, and the gods, led by Indra, sing to the goddess. Partway through comes a line that plays on her name. In paraphrase: you are Durga, the boat across the hard-to-cross ocean of worldly life. Her name, Durga, sits right beside durga, hard to cross, the word the gods use for that ocean. The one named for what is hard to get through is the boat that gets people through it. Some readers hear the name point two ways. Toward anyone who opposes her, she is hard to get past, like a wall. Toward anyone in trouble, she is the way through. That's a good lens for the first nights. Clearing doesn't only mean fighting. Sometimes the obstacle is pushed aside; sometimes it's crossed. In the story the gods asked for help, and the help was both: a wall against what threatened them, and a way across. Some devotees spend these first nights on the battle side of the goddess, the Devi Mahatmya's demons read as anger, pride and confusion, and the nights as a time to face them. Others put the weight on the boat: the goddess as refuge, the one who carries people across. Some families do a little of each, with a fast, a lamp, a reading, a visit to a temple. The second night asks a quiet question. Of the things in your way right now, which need a wall, and which need a boat?
screen: `THE GODS SING AFTER THE VICTORY.` · `DURGA, BESIDE HARD TO CROSS.` · `THE BOAT ACROSS THE HARD OCEAN.` · `A WALL, AND A WAY THROUGH.` · then, large: `WHICH NEEDS A WALL, WHICH A BOAT?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing in your way this week and look at it plainly, then ask: does this need a wall, a no, a limit, a door that stays shut, or a boat, help to get through it, a person to lean on, time to cross? No need to decide tonight. If you pray, you can bring it to Durga, or to God, in your own words; if you don't, let the question be the whole practice.

1111.title: Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum
1111.hook: night three closes the clearing nights: the gods are offered a boon, and ask for something you can use again
1111.howItsDone: Some devotees recite chapters of the Devi Mahatmya during Navaratri, or in times of trouble, holding to the gods' boon in chapter four that the goddess will come when she is remembered.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-ELEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday was night two of Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum: Durga, hard to pass, and the boat across. Tonight, night three.
screen: `A WALL, OR A BOAT.`

segments.voice: Choose a boon. The path heard the goddess say it to the gods earlier this year, reading the Devi Mahatmya whole. The buffalo demon is dead, and the gods could ask for anything: riches, safety forever, a share of her power. Tonight is night three, the last of the clearing nights that, in one way of counting, belong to Durga. And that old request, from the end of the fourth chapter, comes back with a new job. Inside a nine-night course, it's a lesson about coming back.
screen: `CHOOSE A BOON.` → `HEARD BEFORE.` → `NOW, A LESSON ABOUT COMING BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's their answer, in paraphrase. Everything has already been done for us, they say, because our enemy is dead. But if you'll give us a boon, then whenever we remember you again, destroy our worst troubles. And be gracious to anyone who praises you with these hymns. The goddess agrees, and vanishes. Look at what they didn't ask for: not a fortress that would last forever, not a guarantee that nothing bad would happen again. As if they know it will. Heaven has been lost once; it can be lost twice. So they ask for something you can use again. Not a single rescue, but a promise of return: remember me, and I'll come. That's what makes it the right close for the first stretch. Clearing isn't a chore done once and crossed off a list. The road fills up again: clutter, worries, the same old anger. What the first nights teach is not a final cleanup but a way of returning, the habit of remembering the one who clears. Some devotees take the line literally: in trouble, they recite these chapters, or simply say the goddess's name. Others read it inwardly: the remembering is itself the clearing, the moment a person stops and turns toward something larger than the mess in front of them. And it widens the circle. The gods don't ask only for themselves, but for anyone who sings these hymns. Three nights in, the first lesson is learned: what clears the road once can be called on again.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing that has crowded your road these three nights, a worry, a task, a grudge, and on an out-breath let it be set to one side, just for now, noticing the little room it leaves. Then think of what you'd turn to when it comes back: a name, a person, a breath like this one. If you pray, you can say the goddess's name, or the name you use, once, as the remembering; if you don't, let the breath be what you return to.

1112.title: Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum
1112.hook: night four: the list in the Devi Kavacha reaches Kushmanda, and in another way of keeping the festival, Durga's nights give way to Lakshmi's
1112.howItsDone: Some Hindus honor one of the nine forms of Durga named in the Devi Kavacha on each night of Navaratri; others, especially in parts of South India, give three nights each to Durga, Lakshmi and Saraswati.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-TWELVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday was night three of Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum: the gods' boon, and the close of the clearing nights. Tonight the lesson turns.
screen: `NIGHT THREE, DONE.` · `NIGHT FOUR.`

segments.voice: There's a short hymn called the Devi Kavacha, the goddess's armor, which some people recite before the Devi Mahatmya. Partway through, it counts the goddess out like stairs. First, Shailaputri. Second, Brahmacharini. Third, Chandraghanta. Fourth, Kushmanda. And on, name after name, until it says these are the nine Durgas. In some homes that list becomes the festival's calendar: one form for each night. But a second way of keeping Navaratri gives the first three nights to Durga, the middle three to Lakshmi, and the last three to Saraswati. By that count, night four is a hinge.
screen: `THE DEVI KAVACHA COUNTS HER OUT.` → `FOURTH: KUSHMANDA.` → `NIGHT FOUR IS A HINGE.`

segments.voice: Start with Kushmanda; you met her briefly on day ninety-four. The Kavacha only names her; it doesn't tell her story. But there's a story people tell. Before anything existed there was only darkness, and the goddess smiled, and the world came out of that smile. Whatever you make of it, it's a bright picture for the fourth night: light that begins as a face lighting up. Now the second way of counting. Durga's three nights were the clearing nights. You can't plant a garden in a field full of rocks, so the curriculum starts by moving rocks. Then, on night four, Lakshmi arrives: the goddess of good fortune, of plenty, of a household that has enough to share. Earlier this year, the Sri Sukta asked her to come and stay. The order matters: clearing first, then filling. Some families have a homely version: before welcoming Lakshmi, they clean the house, sweep the corners, light the lamp in a clean doorway. A guest like that, they say, comes to a room that's ready. So night four asks a quieter question than the first three. They asked what has to go. Tonight asks what you're making room for. Not more stuff. Enough: health, a full table, friends at it, a little to give away. And Kushmanda's smile sits over all of it, a reminder that in this story the good world begins with delight.
screen: `FOURTH NIGHT: KUSHMANDA.` · `A WORLD FROM A SMILE.` · `DURGA CLEARS, LAKSHMI FILLS.` · `WHAT ARE YOU MAKING ROOM FOR?` · then, large: `CLEARING FIRST, THEN FILLING.`

segments.voice: Notice the room you're sitting in, the space around you and above you, the quiet between sounds, and let it feel roomy. Then let one good thing into that room, a person you're grateful for, a meal you're glad of, something already given, and let it sit there and be enough. If you pray, you can say the goddess's name, or the name you use, quietly with the breath.

1113.title: Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum
1113.hook: night five: dolls climb a set of steps in a living room, and the goddess of the night is a mother with her child on her lap
1113.howItsDone: In parts of South India, families set out a golu (kolu or bombe habba), a display of dolls on steps, for Navaratri and visit each other's homes in the evenings; where the nine forms are kept, the fifth night honors Skandamata.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-THIRTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday was night four of Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum: Kushmanda, and the turn from clearing to filling. Tonight closes a week.
screen: `CLEARING FIRST, THEN FILLING.` · `NIGHT FIVE.`

segments.voice: In a living room in Chennai, someone has built a staircase out of planks and covered it with a cloth. On the steps stand dolls: gods near the top, saints and sages lower, then a wedding procession, a market, a cricket match, tiny clay animals. On the floor, a child has made a park out of sand, with a mirror for a pond. In parts of South India this is the golu, or kolu, set up for Navaratri. In the evenings neighbors come to see it, someone sings, and visitors leave with a small gift. And tonight, the fifth name in the Kavacha's list is a mother holding her child.
screen: `A STAIRCASE OF DOLLS.` → `NEIGHBORS COME TO SEE.` → `THE FIFTH NAME: A MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Her name is Skandamata, the mother of Skanda. Skanda is the son of Shiva and Parvati, a young warrior god, known in the Tamil country as Murugan and elsewhere as Kartikeya. In paintings of this night she sits with the boy on her lap. Notice what the name does. It doesn't call her by her own power. It calls her by the child she holds. Families do this too: a woman becomes so-and-so's mother at the school gate, and she answers to it. The festival that honors the goddess who rides into battle also honors her sitting still with a baby. In this way of keeping it, fierce and tender belong to one goddess. The golu steps make a similar point with dolls. The gods are on them, but so are weddings, vegetable sellers, schoolchildren and cows: the whole ordinary world, set out on the stairs, and people come into each other's homes to look at it. A festival about the goddess turns out to be full of visiting, feeding and children. That's a good place to end a week that began with the Lalita Sahasranama's own story and its last names, then the three clearing nights, then Kushmanda and the turn toward filling, and now a mother with her child. Halfway through, the lesson so far: the power that clears the road is also the power that holds you.
screen: `SKANDAMATA, MOTHER OF SKANDA.` · `CALLED BY THE CHILD SHE HOLDS.` · `FIERCE AND TENDER, ONE GODDESS.` · `THE WHOLE WORLD ON THE STEPS.` · then, large: `THE POWER THAT HOLDS YOU.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who looked after you when you were small, or someone who looks after you now, and stay with one moment of being cared for: a hand on your back, a plate put in front of you. Then, if it comes easily, let it turn around, and think of someone you hold, in whatever way you hold them. If you pray, you can offer both of them to the goddess, or to God, in your own words.
